newsitem.title: USA: Three U.S. soldiers charged in Army sex probe.
newsitem.headline: Three U.S. soldiers charged in Army sex probe.

text.p: Three drill sergeants at a Missouri training base have been charged and at least seven others suspended in a newly disclosed probe of sexual misconduct in the military, the Army said on Tuesday.

The Army said charges ranging from consensual intercourse to indecent assault were brought against three noncommissioned officers at Fort Leonard Wood in south-central Missouri. It said the charges resulted from ongoing investigations and were not related to the unfolding rape and sexual harassment scandal at Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland.

Col. Carl Strock, chief of staff at Fort Leonard Wood, told reporters at a news conference Tuesday that the cases were "disturbing," but that the Army still had confidence in its procedures and its chain of command.
"We acknowledge that we must do better," Strock said. "Sexual harassment is an area of zero tolerance but unfortunately, as in any human enterprise, we are not a zero-defect institution."

Courts martial were pending in the three new cases, with one scheduled to begin on Tuesday and the others due to start within the next month. The Army said other allegations of misconduct at the base were under investigation.
"The three cases ... came to light under the Army's existing policies. They did not surface as a result of the Army's recently established hotline," the Army said in a statement.

Unlike the Maryland investigation, none of the Missouri cases involved charges of rape or forcible sodomy. The alleged offences occurred between the summers of 1995 and 1996 and appeared to be unrelated, the Army said.
Gen. John Shalikashvili, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Monday described the unfolding scandal in Maryland as a "great tragedy" and vowed to prosecute wrongdoers.

Last week three male Army trainers were charged in a rape and sexual harassment case involving alleged attacks on women recruits in Maryland. About 20 people have been suspended from their duties at the Maryland base pending an investigation into the allegations.

Pentagon officials fear the scandal will give the U.S. military another black eye after a string of harassment cases that began with the 1991 "Tailhook" scandal, in which male Navy and Marine pilots fondled women at a Las Vegas hotel.
